extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of mass communication, journalists, political communicators, and readers interested in public opinion
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how images, narratives, and appeals must be constructed to attract, engage, and shape mass audiences and public opinion. Emphasizes visualization, identification, suspense, stereotypes, and the plurality of selves in reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pictures/visualization
rubrics_metrics.description: Pictures have always been the surest way of conveying an idea, and next in order, words that call up pictures in memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer imagery that creates clear visual impressions; if the communicator lacks pictorial skill, employ gifted visualizers. Visualizations capture stimuli and outcomes well but may caricature internal or intermediate states (anti-pattern: overreliance on pictorial rendering for subtle inwardness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification (empathy) with the image
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea conveyed is not fully our own until we have identified ourselves with some aspect of the picture; popular representation almost always marks handles for identification so the audience 'knows who the hero is at once.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make identification cues definite and recognizable (clear hero/role). In popular media, subtle or ambiguous identification reduces broad appeal; sophisticated works can use subtler forms of empathy but risk narrower audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide active engagement (give the audience 'something to do')
rubrics_metrics.description: The audience must have something to do; mere contemplation of the true, the good and the beautiful does not exercise the audience—images should allow the audience to take sides and participate imaginatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design narratives/images that invite the audience to take part (e.g., choose sides, imagine acting). Anti-pattern: static or purely contemplative presentations that fail to provoke an imaginative response will hold attention for few.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit primal motifs (sexual passion and fighting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two forms of exercise that most easily and eagerly arouse audiences are sexual passion and fighting; a fight about sex has especially broad appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use motifs tied to basic drives and conflict to arouse wide interest. Note cultural/jurisdictional limits (e.g., sexual motif figures less in some political imagery); overuse risks sensationalism but is highly effective for mass appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create suspense via struggle and unfolding events
rubrics_metrics.description: Depict unfolding events and struggle; the element of struggle constitutes suspense and holds audience attention—motion pictures draw and retain audiences because they show unfolding events whose outcome is awaited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure narratives to present obstacles, antagonists, and unanswered questions that sustain suspense. Anti-pattern: static masterpieces lacking an unfolding struggle tend to draw smaller, shorter attention from mass audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic beginning and romantic (desirable) ending
rubrics_metrics.description: Popular taste prefers a drama that begins in a realistic setting plausible for identification and ends in a romantic setting desirable but not inconceivable; the realistic start and happy ending are landmarks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor the story in familiar reality to allow entry, then resolve toward an uplifting or desirable conclusion. Avoid pure fantasy (no familiar foothold) or relentless realism (audiences dislike persistent defeat).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to prevailing stereotypes (or change them only cautiously)
rubrics_metrics.description: What will be accepted as true, realistic, good, evil, or desirable is fixed by stereotypes acquired from earlier experience; makers must usually adhere to stereotypes or risk frustrating expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For commercial success, conform to prevalent stereotypes; pioneering artists can alter stereotypes but face commercial risk and delayed public acceptance (example: pioneering works that become new stereotypes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mark heroes, antagonists, and obstacles clearly to produce suspense
rubrics_metrics.description: In popular representation the handles for identification are almost always marked; if a plot lacks suspense, add an antagonist, obstacle, or problem and emphasize questions in the spectator's mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly present protagonists/antagonists and obstacles to create stakes. The footnoted checklist: add an antagonist, add an obstacle, add a problem, emphasize central questions—absence of these is an anti-pattern for popular engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for multiple selves — know which self you engage
rubrics_metrics.description: A person does not have one fixed self; which self is engaged (e.g., patriot, parent, employer) greatly affects how a story is received and what passions are aroused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which aspect(s) of an audience's identity you intend to activate (e.g., domestic provider vs. outraged family head). Messages should be tailored to the relevant self — failing to do so leads to unpredictable reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalize for mixed audiences (use more abstract common factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: As the audience grows larger and more mixed, the number of common words diminishes and common factors in a story become more abstract; the story's particulars will be reinterpreted by varied characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For wide, heterogeneous audiences, favor abstraction and broadly recognizable themes rather than narrowly detailed particulars; expect diverse reinterpretations of specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume simple economic determinism of opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic position limits or enlarges the range of opinions but does not determine which opinions a person will hold; the materialistic conception cannot predict specific beliefs or policy stances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming that class or economic role maps directly to predictable opinions; empirical inquiry is required to learn which of a person's multiple relations shape a particular attitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare audiences morally/intellectually for modern complexities
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral education should prepare characters for the many situations of modern life; moralists must either provide practical patterns of conduct for complex modern situations or prevent people from encountering them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When communicating about modern social/political issues, incorporate realistic moral or practical frameworks (economics, politics, psychology) so audiences can form usable patterns of conduct; failing to educate leaves audiences unprepared.
